title: Jefferson sees AI investment lifting demand before productivity expands supply
summary: Vice Chair Philip Jefferson separated two effects of a technological boom that arrive at different times. Data-centre spending and wealth gains linked to enthusiasm about AI were already supporting demand. Large and lasting additions to productive capacity were plausible, but he expected them more gradually. Until supply caught up, the demand for scarce inputs such as memory chips could lift particular prices and pressure resources more broadly. He had supported the October rate hold. With employment near his assessment of maximum, he gave the inflation trajectory greater near-term weight and declined to specify a future rate change.

The comparison with earlier computing investment is a guide to measurement. In 1989, 32 percent of workers were using computers, yet the machines had limited capacity and spending on them was small. Figure 1 sets each spending series equal to 100 in 2017, showing how rapidly each grew from its own base. The chart uses separate series for business computers, household computers and household phones. Research subsequently attributed about three-quarters of a percentage point of annual labour productivity growth in the late 1990s to investment in IT capital. A second stage came when businesses reorganised around cheaper computing, raising output per unit of combined inputs. Counting new equipment measures capital deepening. It does not capture all organisational gains, and recording an asset purchase does not establish that those gains have happened.

Adoption varies with the population being counted and how frequently it uses AI. In August 2026, 40.55% of surveyed working adults reported using AI at work and 11.47% reported daily use. Both measures declined from May (Figure 2). Figure 3 weights industry observations by establishment counts and excludes firms assigned to multiple industry codes. In early October its total was 24.6%, ranging from 11.38% in natural resources and mining to 46.4% in information. A separate study in note 13 estimated 95% adoption among US firms when weighted by employment. A large employer’s adoption in one function can coexist with occasional use among its workers.

Large gains in an experiment can translate into smaller gains for a business if the task occupies little staff time or generates additional work. Code produced quickly may need more debugging. In the separate survey of managers cited in note 16, the employment-weighted estimate was a half-percent gain in sales per employee over three years. The measure describes a cumulative change in sales per employee. It does not establish an annual rate of aggregate productivity growth.

Labour productivity grew 2.2 percent per year on average in 2020–25 against 1.5 percent in the previous business cycle. The improvement began before mainstream generative chatbots appeared, and new business formation was another candidate explanation. Jefferson consequently judged the contribution of AI to aggregate productivity so far limited and its future size uncertain. He also raised the question of the neutral real interest rate. If firms want more funds to invest while households save less against higher future income, the rate balancing the two could rise. The historical relationship between productivity and real rates is noisy, and he supplied no numerical change to the neutral rate. There is a further distinction for GDP forecasts. Imported IT equipment reduces the immediate contribution of domestic investment spending to US output. Once installed it can still raise output per worker in the United States (note 18). A rise in orders, domestic value added during construction and the later flow of productive services can therefore follow quite different paths.

Figure 4 shows real GDP growth of 3.4 percent at an annualised quarter-on-quarter rate in 2026 Q3. Its earlier bars compare half-years. October unemployment stood at 4.1 percent (Figure 5). He put September twelve-month headline and core PCE inflation at 3.6% and 3.1% respectively. Figure 6’s table reports 3.65% and 3.12%. Energy costs and technology-related input demand were visible in specific categories. Near-term expectations were elevated, while most measures of long-horizon expectations remained consistent with the objective. He judged growth and employment risks broadly balanced. His own medium-term baseline of growth near potential still left room for worker displacement faster than retraining, an outcome whose structural component could limit how much easier monetary policy could remedy.

questions.question: Are investment and consumption advancing faster than new productive capacity?
questions.detail: Compare data-centre construction and equipment orders with utilisation, measured output per hour, revisions to productivity and the diffusion of adoption across industries. Rising equipment prices can signal bottlenecks while broader productivity gains are still ahead. Use the dated BEA releases behind the output and investment series so that later revisions do not become apparent advance evidence. Compare imported equipment with US production before estimating domestic demand pressure. For the later supply effect, follow installation and use across both groups.

questions.question: What connects a successful task experiment to an improvement in a firm’s margins or output?
questions.detail: Measure total labour time including review, correction and reorganisation. Compare adopters with comparable firms and track adoption intensity and client outcomes. Surveyed use in one function and sustained cost savings across an enterprise are different results. Reweight the Census business survey by establishments and by employees before interpreting industry-wide exposure.

questions.question: Is higher potential growth changing the neutral real rate or only current financing demand?
questions.detail: Track investment plans, saving behaviour and longer-horizon real yields across periods with different adoption intensity. Separate policy-rate expectations and term premia, and examine outcomes after construction has finished. Jefferson cites competing historical estimates. Check sensitivity to the chosen inflation-expectations series and productivity-growth horizon.

questions.question: Could employment disruption be structural rather than cyclical?
questions.detail: Compare job-finding duration, vacancy requirements and wage changes for affected occupations with broader demand indicators. Changes in hiring beyond AI-exposed activities would make a sectoral mismatch an incomplete account.

limitation: Jefferson distinguished his own outlook from evidence reported by firms and workers. Figure 7’s accessible table repeats 2025 dates for its last two rows, so the October policy decision is taken from the speech text.
